source.title: EgoScale: Scaling Dexterous Manipulation with Diverse Egocentric Human Data
source.authors: Ruijie Zheng; Dantong Niu; Yuqi Xie; Jing Wang; Mengda Xu; Yunfan Jiang; Fernando Castañeda; Fengyuan Hu; You Liang Tan; Letian Fu; Trevor Darrell; Furong Huang; Yuke Zhu; Danfei Xu; Linxi Fan

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests scaling-like behavior in a new setting: a VLA pretrained on egocentric human video, measuring action-prediction loss against human-data volume and downstream robot performance. It does not reproduce language-model scaling experiments.
record.gate_note: The study tests human-data scaling for action-prediction MSE, not language-model cross-entropy, parameter or compute scaling, or compute-optimal allocation. It reports a log-linear fit against data volume rather than a power-law fit. Other robot-task, action-representation, and embodiment results are not rows because they do not measure the scaling behavior named by these claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study measures held-out action-prediction loss and downstream robot task completion against pretraining data volume (1k–20k hours) in a VLA pretrained on egocentric human video. This is a new, non-text setting with its own scaling result, which bears on V5 and V6. It does not vary parameters or compute, and it does not test allocation, architecture shape or fitting choices.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct in substance. The authors report a near-perfect log-linear relation between data hours and human action-prediction validation loss. They say this loss strongly predicts downstream robot performance, which rises from 0.30 to 0.71 with no saturation in the explored range. They do not extrapolate beyond it. Note, however, that the introduction also says the law 'enables us to extrapolate', which contradicts the later disclaimer.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a VLA pretrained on egocentric human video, with action-prediction MSE measured against data volume. It does not reproduce language-model cross-entropy scaling across parameters, tokens, or compute, nor compute-optimal allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that models trained on 1k–2k hours plateau or degrade later in training, whereas models trained on 10k–20k hours improve steadily without signs of overfitting. No sensitivity to fitting method or fitting choices is tested.
record.problems: The scaling experiment covers five data volumes from 1k to 20k hours and a single VLA setup. The reported fit is for action-prediction MSE, not language-model cross-entropy; no uncertainty estimates or numerical downstream correlation coefficient are given. The authors do not extrapolate beyond the measured range.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant results left out. Other reported task, embodiment, and action-representation comparisons do not measure the scaling behavior in these versions.

untested.parts: Scaling in parameters or compute; image or video generative models; repeated data; fine-tuning and transfer as loss-scaling regimes. Only data volume, in one VLA setup, over 1k–20k hours.
Prediction across model size or compute. A quantitative loss-to-task mapping. Extrapolation beyond the measured range, which the authors explicitly decline to make.
No language-model pretraining loss is measured.

missing.what: Intermediate downstream task-completion values at each data scale: 0.45 (2k), 0.48 (4k), 0.57 (10k). These are needed to judge how smooth or log-linear the downstream trend is.

Validation-loss curves over training. The 1k–2k hour runs plateau or degrade (overfit), while the 10k–20k hour runs keep improving. This is relevant to whether the data-limited loss is measured where other factors are not the bottleneck.

record.verdict_notes: The record's V5 label 'challenges' is too strong. The study never fits or rejects a power law, and over a 20× range a log law and a small-exponent power law are hard to tell apart. So the result qualifies V5 rather than showing it absent. Only data volume is varied: there is one model size and no compute sweep. Downstream evaluation uses two seeds and 10 trials per checkpoint, and no uncertainty is reported. The units of D in Equation 1 appear inconsistent with the plotted values.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test held-out language-model pretraining loss against parameters, tokens, or compute.
Does not test whether small-run fits predict much larger language-model runs; the authors explicitly say they do not extrapolate beyond the measured data range.
No fixed-compute-budget comparison or optimal parameter/token allocation.
No comparison of architecture depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.

Tests egocentric human-video VLA pretraining and action-prediction loss versus data volume only; does not test image or video prediction models, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer regimes as scaling-law loss measurements.
Tests downstream robot task completion after human-data scaling, but does not report a numerical correlation coefficient or test a broad range of downstream task families.
Does not compare fitting methods, parameter-count conventions, training schedules, or compute-optimal allocation fits.

rows.subject: EgoScale VLA checkpoints
rows.operation_detail: Compared optimal held-out human-action prediction loss across pretraining data volumes.

conditions.value: 20 sampled timesteps per trajectory; 16 action samples per timestep, averaged

rows.measure: Held-out human wrist and hand action prediction mean squared error
rows.value: L = 0.024 − 0.003 · ln(D); R² = 0.9983, where D is hours of human pretraining data
rows.note: The reported loss decreases with data volume, but the fitted form is linear in ln(D), not the same power-law form specified in V5. The paper reports an aggregate fit over the five data-volume settings.
rows.check: The state is right: loss falls monotonically with data, but the study fits a log-linear form, not a power law, and compares no alternative form. The value needs a caveat. With D read literally in hours, the fit gives near-zero loss at 1k hours (0.024 − 0.003·ln 1000 ≈ 0.003), while Figure 5 shows about 0.024 there. The constants therefore only match the plot if D is in thousands of hours. The range spans about 1.3 orders of magnitude, and each point is the minimum over training, picked from runs where small datasets overfit.

source_check.problem: Faithfully transcribed, but the source equation has an internal numerical inconsistency; see notes.

rows.subject: EgoScale VLA checkpoints
rows.stage_stated: downstream task post-training after human pretraining
rows.operation_detail: Compared downstream robot performance after pretraining on different amounts of human data.
rows.value: 0.71 at 20k hours; the text says performance rises monotonically across the tested data scales
rows.note: Aggregate endpoint comparison across the data-scale experiment; the paper also describes monotonic improvement between the endpoints.
rows.check: Correct. The 'scale' here is pretraining data volume only; model size and compute are not varied. Only the endpoints are recorded. The intermediate values read from Figure 5 (right) are 0.45 (2k), 0.48 (4k) and 0.57 (10k).

rows.subject: EgoScale VLA checkpoints
rows.stage_stated: human pretraining and downstream robot post-training
rows.operation_detail: Assessed how held-out human-action validation loss relates to downstream robot task completion across data scales.
rows.measure: Relationship between human validation loss and downstream task completion
rows.value: The authors state that validation loss strongly correlates with, and closely tracks, downstream task completion across data scales
rows.note: No numerical correlation coefficient is reported.
rows.check: Based only on the authors' qualitative statement that loss 'closely tracks' task completion. No correlation coefficient or per-scale pairing is given beyond the two figures, and each scale point uses two seeds.

relationships.condition: EgoScale VLA, action-prediction MSE vs. human pretraining data, 1k–20k hours
relationships.reason: Loss falls monotonically and predictably with data (R²=0.9983), but the reported form is log-linear, not a power law, over only ~1.3 orders of magnitude (r1).
relationships.display_finding: Action-prediction loss decreased monotonically with a log-linear fit achieving R²=0.9983 across approximately 1.3 orders of magnitude, rather than a fitted power law.
